name: Medial-entry intramedullary nailing approach to the clavicle
corridor: Small anterior medial-clavicle window into the intramedullary canal for lateral nail passage

positioning.text: Position beach-chair or supine with the shoulder supported, medial clavicle accessible, and arm mobile for indirect reduction.

setup.text: Prepare the full clavicle and arm, template nail diameter and length, and obtain clear fluoroscopic views of the medial entry, fracture, and lateral fragment.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the sternoclavicular joint, medial clavicle, fracture, lateral clavicle, and anticipated anterior nail entry just lateral to the joint.

incision.text: Make a 1–2 cm anterior incision just lateral to the sternoclavicular joint over the medial clavicular entry point.

superficial_interval.text: Bluntly dissect to bone, protecting supraclavicular sensory branches and maintaining direct contact with the anterior clavicle.

deep_interval.text: Create the medial canal entry under direct and fluoroscopic control, then advance the flexible nail along the S-shaped canal without perforating cortex.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue and supraclavicular branches, fascia and periosteum, medial clavicular cortex, then intramedullary canal.

structures_encountered.text: Supraclavicular sensory branches, platysma, medial clavicle, sternoclavicular-adjacent soft tissues, canal, and fracture are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Supraclavicular nerves, sternoclavicular joint, subclavian vessels, brachial plexus, pleura, and skin at the medial nail end are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Do not direct the entry tool or nail posteriorly beyond the far cortex; avoid medial migration toward the sternoclavicular region and intrathoracic structures.

retraction_hazards.text: Use minimal retraction through the small medial window and enlarge it if the entry point cannot be seen directly.

exposure.text: Provides limited medial canal access with indirect fracture reduction and little fracture-site stripping.

limitations.text: The curved canal and comminution can impede passage, rotational control is less direct than plating, and some patterns require a small fracture-site incision.

extensions.text: Add a limited fracture window for reduction or nail passage, or convert to plate fixation when canal passage or stable alignment cannot be achieved.

indications.text: Use for selected displaced midshaft fractures with a canal and pattern suitable for intramedullary fixation; technique choice remains patient- and fracture-specific.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid in markedly comminuted, very medial or lateral, canal-incompatible, pathologic, or irreducible patterns lacking reliable length and rotational control.

implant_implications.text: Select a nail that negotiates the canal without cortical perforation, seat the medial end to minimize skin irritation, and secure it against migration according to device design.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Continuously confirm entry, intramedullary passage, fracture reduction, lateral endpoint, absence of cortical perforation, and final nail position.

closure.text: Irrigate, verify the nail end is not prominent beneath skin, close fascia and skin in layers, and protect the medial entry wound.

complications.text: Complications include cortical perforation, nail migration, medial skin irritation, supraclavicular neuropathy, pneumothorax or neurovascular injury, malalignment, nonunion, infection, and implant removal.

bailouts.text: Stop if the nail leaves the canal or cannot cross safely; use a targeted fracture window, exchange the implant, or convert to plating rather than forcing passage.

procedure_applications.condition: A selected midshaft fracture can be reduced and stabilized with an intramedullary device

questions.question: Where is the standard clavicle nail entry incision?
questions.answer: Anteriorly just lateral to the sternoclavicular joint.

questions.question: What geometric feature makes nail passage difficult?
What must never be accepted during nail passage?
questions.answer: Posterior cortical perforation or extraosseous advancement toward neurovascular and thoracic structures.
